newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cult leader admits faking divinity for money.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cult leader admits faking divinity for money.

text.p: A Taiwan cult leader has admitted to lying about possessing divine powers in a major hoax that conned millions of dollars in cash and gifts out of followers.

Sung Chi-li, who on Sunday morning had denied allegations of fraud and maintained he was the reincarnation of a "cosmic body", made the confession later in the day after being detained by police and failing to demonstrate supernatural powers.
"Please don't believe in me any more," a handcuffed and tearful Sung told followers as police led him through a throng of photographers after more than nine hours of interrogation.
During the questioning, the police asked Sung to prove his divinity through a display of his purported special powers.
After failing to do so, Sung confessed he had swindled millions of dollars in land, cars, and cash from thousands of followers who worshipped him like a god, police said.
Also on Sunday, Taipei officials used heavy equipment to begin demolishing the Sung Chi-li Transmogrification Society's main shrine on grounds that it was built illegally.

Several of Sung's thousands of followers have accused him of defrauding up to T$3 billion (US$109 million) from cult members by convincing them he had supernatural healing powers and could make likenesses of himself appear in many places at one time.

Sung's organisation attracted large followings in Taiwan and the Chinese mainland by using photographs that appeared to show the cult leader with a bright halo or levitating above the Great Wall or over Taiwan.
A cult photographer arrested in the scam admitted to police that he faked the series of pictures to defraud followers.
Sung himself became the fifth person detained in what police suspect was a major fraud ring with possible wider connections to senior Taiwan officials and businessmen.
The others detained are the society's former chairman Chang Nai-jen and current Chairman Hung Ying-lin, photographers Lo Cheng-hung and Cheng Chen-tung.

Frank Hsieh, vice presidential candidate for the opposition Democratic Progressive Party in Taiwan's election last March, has been facing mounting criticism from other political parties and even his own for belonging to and accepting donations from the association on behalf of himself and the party.
Hsieh has denied any wrongdoing but admitted to serving as Sung's attorney.
Local media also have linked Taiwan's deputy police chief Yu Yu-tang to Sung's cult.
Yu has said he knew of Sung, but denied knowing of the organisations' operations.
